new_statements.quote: Transcriptions of data are adapted to IPA standards, with the following exceptions. The letter ‹y› is used for the palatal glide [j], Tarangan mid-close [e] and [o] are transcribed ‹ê› and ‹ô› (mid-open [ɛ] and [ɔ] are transcribed ‹ɛ› and ‹ɔ›), and unexpected stress is marked by an acute accent. (The normal pattern is penultimate stress, or final stress if the final syllable contains a mid-vowel.)
new_statements.citation: Grimes, Charles E. & Owen Edwards. 2026. The Austronesian languages of eastern Indonesia and Timor-Leste: unravelling their prehistory and classification. Berlin: Language Science Press (langsci 526).
new_statements.locator: Grimes & Edwards 2026, ch. 6 Aru, p.273 (also sec. 2, pp.87-88 quoting Nivens 2017)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: statement check: group-level-statement. lines 5767-5772 (pp.87-88) attribute the note to Nivens (2017) 'in the comparative Aru data.. unexpected stress is marked by an acute accent (the normal pattern is penultimate stress, or final stress if the final syllable contains a mid-vowel)', repeated at ch.6 p.273 (lines 14267-14272) for all Aru data. It is an Aru-wide transcription default taken from Nivens' database, not a Kompane analysis; Kompane rows do carry acutes only on exceptions (e.g. ngamá, gwáel), so the default applies to Kompane by convention. | checker: Grimes & Edwards 2026 (langsci 526) full text held by the project (boan1242/): ch. 6 'Aru' opens p.273 with the transcription note…
new_statements.relation_note: States that for the Aru data the normal (unmarked) pattern is penultimate stress, or final stress if the final syllable contains a mid vowel; deviations carry an acute accent (e.g. Barakai gamár, ʤágel, da-bálar).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress penultimate; final if the last syllable has a mid vowel (e/o); other placements lexical and marked with an acute in the data.
new_statements.exceptions: final stress when the final syllable contains a mid vowel; individually marked words with acute accent
new_statements.identity_note: group-level statement: a transcription convention stated for all Aru data in the chapter (Nivens 2017 database, Hughes/Daigle/Schapper field lists); Kompane is one of the Aru languages tabulated (map Fig. 6.1, tables 6.x). [name in source: Kompane; pages ch. 6 'Aru', p.273 (transcription conventions, from Nivens 2017; restated pp.87-88); Kompane forms in Tables 6.x; p.273 'Karey, Lorang, Mariri, and Kompane are only spoken in one village each']

sources.citation: Takata, Masahiro & Yuko Takata. 1992. Kola phonology. In Donald A. Burquest & Wyn D. Laidig (eds.), Descriptive studies in languages of Maluku (NUSA 34), 31-46. Jakarta: Universitas Katolik Indonesia Atma Jaya.
sources.note: SISTER LANGUAGE KOLA (kola1285), Kolamar/Marlasi villages, not Kompane. Sec. 2.5 p. 40: 'It is not predictable whether stress occurs on the penultimate or the ultimate syllable of monomorphemic words. Penultimate stress, however, is most common in Kola. It should be noted that stress falls only on the root and never on affixes or clitics. In addition, stress does not occur beyond the penult of the root.' Gives minimal pairs (/'bobah/ 'fear' vs /bo'bo/ 'baby'); stress shifts under resyllabification in compounds; Sec. 4 p. 43 defines the phonological word as a stress group with one primary stre…

sources.note: No prose on stress or tone. The twelve numeral forms are transcribed WITH primary-stress marks: 1 'ʔetu, 2 'rua, 3 'lasi, 4 'kaha, 5 'lima, 6 'dubu, 7 du'bam (lit. '6+1'), 8 kaha'rua ('four two'), 9 'teri, 10 hu'ɸaɸi, 100 'hatu, 1000 hiɸu'nia. Penultimate stress on every polysyllable except du'bam (final; a contracted compound); this is wordlist-only evidence (marks without any statement), consistent with the penult-default pattern Takata & Takata 1992 state for the sister language Kola, but NOT a statement for Kompane. sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2.2.3.3 (p. 98): Kompane spoken by 254 people in one village (Kompane, east coast of Kongan Island); no dialect variation; relates to the nearest Kola village Mohang Sel at 79% and is a 'bridge' between Ujir/Kola and the central Aru chain. Lexicostatistics only.
